subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Authority Bias: Trusting the Lab Coat
description: A 60-second lesson on The Authority Bias: Trusting the Lab Coat.

hook.text: Stanley Milgram asked people to shock strangers.

buildup.text: Authority bias: we defer to perceived authority figures even when their commands conflict with our own judgment.

discovery.text: A lab coat, a title, or a confident tone can override critical thinking. We evolved to follow leaders for survival.

twist.text: Advertisers exploit this: '4 out of 5 doctors recommend...' The doctors may not exist. The claim works anyway.

climax.text: Respecting expertise is rational. Blindly obeying authority is not. The line between them matters enormously.

punchline.text: Trust experts. But never stop asking why.

quiz.question: What did Milgram's experiment reveal about authority?
options: Most people obey authority even against their own judgment

details.summary: Authority bias is the tendency to attribute greater accuracy to the opinions of authority figures regardless of their actual expertise. A lab coat, title, or confident tone can override your own judgment.
details.whyItMatters: Blindly trusting authority leads to following bad medical advice, unquestioning obedience, and accepting claims outside an expert's actual domain.
takeaways: Authority cues like titles and uniforms amplify perceived credibility
Milgram's experiments showed extreme obedience to authority
Always check whether the authority is relevant to the specific claim

faq.question: How can you tell whether an authority figure is credible on a specific topic?
faq.answer: Check whether their expertise matches the claim being made. A Nobel physicist opining on nutrition is speaking outside their domain. Credentials in one field do not transfer authority to another.

faq.question: What did Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments reveal about authority bias?
faq.answer: Milgram showed that ordinary people would deliver what they believed were dangerous electric shocks when instructed by an authority figure in a lab coat. The experiments demonstrated how powerfully authority overrides personal judgment.
